newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian workers may strike "early as next week".
newsitem.headline: Colombian workers may strike "early as next week".

text.p: Colombia's main public sector union could bring forward plans for an indefinite, nationwide strike to "as early as next week" in protest at the government's adoption of emergency economic powers, its leader said Monday.

Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo announced late Monday the first concrete measures of the 20-day emergency, which President Ernesto Samper decreed earlier in the day. Most of the measures were aimed at reining in the burgeoning fiscal deficit and included drastic cuts in new foreign debt.

Wilson Borja Diaz, head of the 800,000-strong FENALTRASE state workers' union, however, feared the government could also slash as many as 19,000 public sector jobs as part of further measures likely to be issued in the coming days.

FENALTRASE announced last week it would fix the date of an indefinite strike on January 20 in protest at the 13.5 percent weighted increase in public sector pay, well below the 1996 inflation level of 21.63 percent. Borja said at the time industrial action would begin about mid-February.
"We had initially been planning to launch a stoppage around mid-February but this decree of emergency powers could force us to bring those plans radically forward," Borja said.
"A strike could start as soon as early next week," he said.
The legal workers' union ASONAL, with strong links to FENALTRASE, has already said it will start a strike Monday in protest at pay levels and labor conditions.
The main oil workers' union USO, whose members are employees of the state-run oil company Ecopetrol, has said it would back the strike call.

But Gustavo Triana, a member of the USO national directorate, said it was not yet clear whether this would totally paralyse all oil-related activities or whether non- unionised staff would continue running operations.

The three main private sector labour federations also seem set to heed the call for a national strike. Leaders, already disgruntled at the below-inflation increase of 21.02 percent in the private sector minimum wage, are scheduled to discuss industrial action at a crisis meeting on Friday.
Samper anticipated union reaction to the emergency decree in a televised speech Monday evening.
"I want to warn you once and for all. Protests and strikes will lead nowhere quite simply because although the government has all the goodwill in the world, it is short of money," he said.
Unions say Samper's government has carried out neoliberal economic policies that have eroded the livelihoods of the working class and poorest in society.
The government has the option of extending the economic emergency, initially decreed for 20 days, to a maximum of 90- days. The government is due to announce further austerity measures on Tuesday.
